title: AI Blood Tests Could Cut Fatty Liver Screening Cost in India
excerpt: AIG Hospitals and ISB say routine blood work screened by AI costs Rs 200-Rs 300 per patient, against Rs 5,000-Rs 6,000 for scans - as a first step, not a diagnosis.
body:
• AIG Hospitals in Hyderabad and the Indian School of Business have built an AI tool that screens for fatty liver from routine blood work for Rs 200-Rs 300 per patient, compared with Rs 5,000-Rs 6,000 for scan-based detection, according to the hospital team.
  • The tool is a screening step, not a diagnosis: people flagged by blood tests still need confirmatory assessment such as FibroScan or specialist review.
  • Reader utility: if you have type 2 diabetes, obesity or abnormal liver enzymes, ask your doctor about a liver function panel and a FIB-4 score first - both use routine blood values - before paying for imaging.
  • Separate research in 1,590 adults with confirmed fatty liver disease found a routine gamma-GT blood test performed better than FIB-4 as a first assessment, but the authors say the approach still needs validation in general populations.

A Hyderabad hospital group says artificial intelligence applied to ordinary blood tests can cut the cost of fatty liver screening in India from thousands of rupees to a few hundred. AIG Hospitals, working with the Indian School of Business (ISB), has developed a model that looks for patterns in routine blood work to identify early markers of fatty liver disease, according to reporting on the project by MedBound Times.

Dr Rakesh Kalapala, senior consultant gastroenterologist and director of AIG's AI and Innovation Centre, put the screening cost at Rs 200-Rs 300 per patient, against Rs 5,000-Rs 6,000 for traditional scan-based detection. The hospital says avoiding scans at the first step could save more than Rs 1.2 crore over time in its own setting. Those are absolute rupee figures for the test itself; they do not include the cost of follow-up imaging or specialist care for people who screen positive.

How the screening works

The model was built by clinicians at AIG together with AI experts under ISB's Max Institute of Healthcare Management initiative. Instead of sending every at-risk patient for imaging, it analyses values already collected in routine blood panels and flags those whose pattern suggests fatty liver. Prof. Sarang Deo of ISB said adoption depends on the tool being fast, safe and reliable inside existing hospital workflows, not just accurate in a trial.

The approach fits a wider shift toward blood-first triage. In the LITMUS programme, researchers assessed blood tests and scanning techniques in 1,590 adults with biopsy-confirmed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) across 13 countries, in research published in The Lancet and reported by Diabetes.co.uk. Gamma-glutamyl transferase, or gamma-GT, performed better than the widely used FIB-4 score as an initial assessment, and the researchers suggested gamma-GT could be followed by an ELF blood test or FibroScan where further investigation was needed.

What the evidence does not yet show

Neither result turns a blood test into a stand-alone diagnosis. The LITMUS researchers found that identifying advanced scarring was more straightforward than identifying active inflammatory disease, known as MASH; only the SOMAScan panel reached the study's predefined accuracy threshold for at-risk MASH, and liver biopsy may still be needed for some decisions. The study also recruited people already known to have MASLD and under specialist investigation. In a general population, where advanced disease is less common in absolute terms, the same test will produce a different mix of true and false positives, which is why the researchers say further validation is required before screening pathways change.

AIG's own figures are preliminary internal trial results reported by the hospital, including a claim that the tool improved diagnostic clarity and communication by over 90 percent. That is a process measure from the developer, not an independent accuracy rate, and readers should not read it as a 90 percent chance that any individual result is correct.

Who should consider screening, and what to ask

Fatty liver often develops without symptoms, and it is particularly common among people with type 2 diabetes, where insulin resistance and excess liver fat occur together. The practical sequence supported by the sources is: start with routine blood work your doctor orders, including liver enzymes and the values needed for a FIB-4 calculation; if that first step flags risk, expect a second step such as an ELF test or FibroScan; and treat any AI score as a reason for that follow-up, not as a final answer. If you are quoted Rs 5,000-Rs 6,000 for imaging as a first step, ask whether a blood-based assessment at Rs 200-Rs 300, where available, is appropriate in your case first.

AIG says the model, built specifically for Indian clinical settings, is set to be extended to partner hospitals with clinician training. Until independent validation in unselected Indian populations is published, the honest claim is narrower and still useful: blood-first screening can lower the entry cost of finding people who need a closer look.
